speakers: Cem Karsan (guest, options/vol strategist and wealth manager; called Jim in captions)
Niels Kaastrup Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged)
summary: Karsan, an options/vol strategist, argues cash and margin positioning, record valuations and vol dynamics make markets fragile, and that a structural-inflation, populist regime (1960s-70s analog) favours long vol in metals, FX and bonds. He criticises 60/40 and VIX as a fear gauge, and cites election and midterm patterns in populist periods.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: how we're having a really kind of geopolitical kind of um war underneath the surface, and it really is war.
claims.claim: Russia-Ukraine tanker flows and the Venezuela embargo/tanker seizure are linked, making geopolitics a hot rather than purely economic conflict that matters for oil markets.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: what tends to not be as quick moving is actual positioning, cash positioning. It tends to move a little slower.
claims.claim: Survey sentiment moves fast but actual cash and margin positioning is slower and is real money, so positioning data is a more reliable read on crowding than sentiment.
claims.testable: partly - positioning series exist, threshold not given

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: cash positioning is uh for for uh your average investor is at the lowest ever. Um below 3%. And margin uh for investing is also at record highs.
claims.claim: Record-low cash (<3%) plus record margin debt plus record valuations leaves equities fragile, since little buying power remains.
claims.indicator: investor cash allocation; margin debt; valuation
claims.conditions: when cash is lowest ever, margin at record and valuations at record
claims.testable: yes - cash/margin/valuation extremes can be tested vs forward returns

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup Larsen
claims.quote: average cash allocations among European investors has fallen to now only 2.8%. That's the lowest in 12 years.
claims.claim: BofA survey shows record net bullishness on European equities (net 92% see 12-month upside), cash at 2.8% (12-year low) and the highest equity/commodity exposure since Feb 2022, i.e. crowded risk-on positioning.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup Larsen
claims.quote: the exposure to tech stocks is at the highest level uh as well. And AI stocks now, I think, is something like 40% of the US equity markets or something like that.
claims.claim: Tech/AI exposure is at record concentration (AI about 40% of US equities), adding to crowding risk.
claims.indicator: tech/AI share of index; survey tech exposure

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the VIX measures at-the-money uh implied volatility. And naturally, low the lower the market goes, you slide to a higher implied volatility.
claims.claim: The VIX rises mechanically as the market falls because at-the-money vol slides up the skew, so its rise alone does not show fear.
claims.testable: yes - decompose VIX into skew-slide vs fixed-strike change

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: see how they were moving on implied vol relative to their strike, or in other words, fixed strike vol. That is the the best fear indicator out there.
claims.claim: Fixed-strike implied vol (change in vol of each option holding strike constant) is a better fear and risk indicator than the VIX.
claims.indicator: fixed-strike implied vol of S&P options

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: compression of vol during these quarterly OPEX weeks, the week leading into it and the week of
claims.claim: Around big quarterly (especially year-end) OPEX, structured-product and option positioning compresses vol in the week before and week of expiry.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: it is much more likely to see higher uh prices on a fixed strike basis.
claims.claim: After the OPEX-related supply of vol diminishes, buyers step in and fixed-strike vol is more likely to rise, so the compression is a buying point for vol.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: one of the best trades in when I started in the business in '98, '99, 2000, 2001, 2002 for a four four or five-year period was really to be uh long out-of-the-money uh calls
claims.claim: In the 1998-2002 bubble, long ~25-delta calls three months or more out (stock replacement, even hedged with short stock net long a little delta) beat owning stock because markets rose with vol up.
claims.direction: long OTM calls instead of stock
claims.conditions: bubble regimes with rising vol; not very short-dated options
claims.testable: partly - one episode, needs definition of bubble regime

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the the bigger moves happen at the end. Um, and then eventually it's a bubble and it ends.
claims.claim: Late in a bubble the biggest, fastest moves occur and volatility rises, so the payoff distribution becomes more leptokurtic on both tails.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: why own the whole asset when you can just own the right tail, which is by by the way the cheapest thing in in implied implied vol basis on the curve.
claims.claim: The upside tail (OTM calls) is the cheapest part of the implied vol surface, so owning the right tail is better value than owning the asset when outcomes become leptokurtic.
claims.indicator: OTM call implied vol vs ATM
claims.conditions: when the return distribution is expected to fatten on the right tail

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The long-term average of at-the-money vol is about a 17 uh vol.
claims.claim: A 25-delta S&P call priced near 12 vol is at a discount to the roughly 17 long-term average ATM vol, which makes it cheap (negative risk premium) in a bubble.
claims.indicator: S&P 25-delta call implied vol vs 17 long-run ATM vol
claims.testable: yes - compare implied vs long-run average

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we have seen significant support to longer-term vol.
claims.claim: After a fixed-strike implied vol low in August, longer-dated vol found support and the desk saw vol buying opportunities for the next three months.
claims.testable: partly - claim of a past call

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Uh we are definitely playing from the long vol side on the right tail.
claims.claim: Desk view: stay long vol on the right tail and monetize on the 5% pullbacks while implied vol is likely higher into year-end.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: value quality focused over the long term cuz that reduces volatility, even though long-term returns are similar to growth uh things.
claims.claim: Value/quality stocks have lower volatility than growth with similar long-run returns, which improves risk-adjusted return.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: as interest rates go higher, multiple contraction is an issue for equities.
claims.claim: Rising rates compress equity multiples, so equities are hurt by higher rates through valuation.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: interest rates are generally tied to inflation, higher inflation means higher costs, which reduces profit margins.
claims.claim: For most companies margins fall as rates rise because rates track inflation and inflation raises costs.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: There are a sub- subset, about 25%, a significant minority, um that that do the opposite.
claims.claim: About 25% of companies, notably negative-working-capital businesses such as insurers and many financials, see margins improve as rates and inflation rise because they get cash upfront, pay later and face fewer competitors.
claims.indicator: negative working capital; margin sensitivity to rates
claims.testable: yes - sort stocks by working capital and test

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Middleman businesses don't have more costs. Volume goes up, they do well.
claims.claim: Transactional or distributor businesses (card networks, banks, Coca-Cola) benefit in inflation because nominal volumes rise without proportional cost increases.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: a rising long into the curve. And a and importantly, a steepening curve.
claims.claim: Buffett's top holdings (banks, insurers, energy, distributors) are positioned for rising long rates and a steeper yield curve, which is a risk-management play.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if there's one company that's a major that will benefit, it's Chevron, actually.
claims.claim: Chevron is the major most likely to benefit from Venezuela developments because it has existing Venezuelan operations.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you can use the brakes to go around the turns, you can accelerate, then you're in control, there's less risk, and you can go faster on average. You can add leverage.
claims.claim: Good risk management (diversification, quality) lets you apply leverage and earn higher returns, rather than just taking less risk.
claims.direction: add leverage to a higher-Sharpe portfolio
claims.testable: yes - compare levered high-Sharpe vs unlevered

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Bonds are not a diversifier to stocks. They do not reduce your risk. It is just a matter of taking the speed down of the portfolio.
claims.claim: 60/40 just lowers total risk and return at the same Sharpe ratio; bonds do not diversify stocks.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup Larsen
claims.quote: I think it's somewhere between 1 and 1/2 and two times leverage.
claims.claim: Buffett's record includes about 1.5-2x leverage and steep drawdowns, so his returns are not just stock picking.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: When you when you get to a two Sharpe by diversification or other measures of managing risk, um then you lose use leverage, and that's how you get outsize returns.
claims.claim: Hedge funds first raise Sharpe through diversification and risk control, then use leverage to create outsize returns; without leverage Buffett-like quality only lowers risk.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup Larsen
claims.quote: take people's annualized volatility. I mean people, so investment strategies and divided it by their maximum drawdown.
claims.claim: Dividing max drawdown by annualized vol shows tail risk that Sharpe hides; smooth-looking strategies can have drawdown/vol ratios far larger than expected.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: because drawdowns are rarer, you have less data on drawdowns and people can have 5 10-year track records with great Sharps, but have tremendous tails of the portfolio.
claims.claim: Drawdowns are rare so a 5-10 year track record with a good Sharpe can hide large tail risk until it hits.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: You really want area under the curve with some measure adjusting for you know amount of size as well.
claims.claim: Prefer a risk measure that penalizes bigger losses (Sortino or area under the drawdown curve) over Sharpe, which treats upside and downside vol alike.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: I think the difference is nowadays the structural flows of buyers versus sellers is just much bigger than it's ever been relative to other flows.
claims.claim: Structural (non-opinion) flows are now larger and more measurable than ever, so understanding market microstructure and positioning gives an edge.
claims.testable: partly - flows are hard to measure fully

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: So understand that positioning, understand the effects that that positioning will have as it is either unwound or as as hedging to those positioning kind of are done.
claims.claim: To anticipate regime shifts, estimate who is positioned and how that positioning will be unwound or hedged; reflexivity arises from these reaction functions.
claims.testable: partly - positioning data coverage is limited

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: those flows generally mean reverting to some some reality and that generally happens as liquidity comes out of the system at some point.
claims.claim: Short-term positioning drives moves for days to 2 years, but over 5-10 years flows mean-revert as liquidity leaves, with timing hard to predict.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if you can collect that data and have a good sense of what some positioning is or broad positioning. You don't have to know everything.
claims.claim: Rough positioning data plus a model of how holders react is enough; the reaction function is what is solved for.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: that'll tell you then what the reactionary flows should be.
claims.claim: For options, time decay, vol changes and spot moves mechanically produce hedging flows that can be inferred from positioning.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Generally speaking, the reflexive effects on implied volatility are much stronger.
claims.claim: Positioning has stronger effects on implied vol than on the underlying because vol is less liquid, so the path of implied vol is easier to predict from positioning.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: They are important for it for the move, the direction, but they during some periods are significantly smaller and even when they're bigger are maybe 40% at at the best.
claims.claim: Delta flows from option hedging (gamma, vanna, charm) explain at best about 40% of direction and are sometimes much smaller.
claims.testable: yes - regress returns on flow estimates

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: I do think the distributional effects of implied vol compression and the those are much more predictable and much more powerful and easy easy to use.
claims.claim: Predicting the distribution (vol compression/expansion) is more reliable than predicting direction from option flows.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Um you know, we've had this very clear broad thesis about structural inflation and populism, right?
claims.claim: Karsan's structural-inflation and populism thesis led to calls on gold and gold vol (gold at 2500, buy 3000 calls) years ago.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the way it was performing relative to all other commodities was completely out of line with that.
claims.claim: Gold lagged other commodities despite being the best asset for structural inflation, so the gap was a relative-value opportunity in precious metals, not a broad commodities call.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you want to sell puts in in oil. Uh collect that premium and go plow it into as many long calls in gold as you can.
claims.claim: Sell oil puts and buy gold calls with the premium: a near zero-cost trade that gains convexity to gold while collecting premium in oil.
claims.direction: short oil vol, long gold vol
claims.conditions: structural inflation regime; does not pay every year

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the inflation of the '60s and '70s had four different bouts. It was not one secular move.
claims.claim: Structural inflation comes in cyclical waves, so a long-term inflation view must tolerate months-long inflation lulls.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: During '60s and '70s, precious metals were not only the best performing asset, most people know that, but it was the most volatile asset.
claims.claim: In the 1960s-70s, precious metals were both the best-performing and most volatile asset.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: its implied vol simultaneously at the lows on a risk-adjusted basis, that was one of the most ridiculous trades.
claims.claim: With precious metals vol at lows relative to other assets while the best asset was the most volatile, long gold vol was very cheap.
claims.indicator: gold implied vol vs other assets

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: over that decade 14 years '68 to '82, it went nowhere in nominal terms. So talk about implied vol compression.
claims.claim: Equity index went nowhere nominally from 1968-82, so equity implied vol compressed in that regime.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Uh that FX vol is the way to go. I've been saying it for four or five years.
claims.claim: FX vol (and precious metals, which trade like FX) should be long in the structural inflation regime.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: precious metals, FX, bond vol dramatically higher on all time frames. And then you go look at equity vol. Long-term vol equity dramatically lower.
claims.claim: Regime rule: precious metal, FX and bond vol rise on all horizons, while long-dated equity vol falls (short-term only in line).
claims.direction: long metals/FX/bond vol, short long-dated equity vol

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: multiples should contract cuz as interest rates go higher, multiples need to contract to stay in line with that.
claims.claim: Structurally rising rates and inflation force equity multiples down.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: structurally if you're selling out of the money puts, a much safer play.
claims.claim: Industrial commodities are capped by deglobalization and spiked by inflation, so selling OTM puts (not calls) in energy is safer.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: This is a structural cycle. Uh the populist is populism is, which is a function of inequality.
claims.claim: Populism is the outcome of an inequality cycle, so this is not a sample of one; it provides a structural basis for the 1960s-70s analogy.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: because when you are young, you are labor. And when you retire and you're old, you're capital.
claims.claim: Inequality expansion is felt unequally across generations; young labor is disenfranchised while the old own capital, which drives political change.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: it's not good for predicting one-year, two-year outcomes or five-year outcomes, but if you're looking at 80-year, 40-year, 20-year, decade outcomes, it's incredibly valuable to understand those dynamics.
claims.claim: The inequality/populism cycle is useful for decade-scale outcomes but not for 1-5 year forecasts.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: you want to be able to do things that you measure. Those are the things that are the best for prediction that can give you great conviction.
claims.claim: Base views on measurable structural drivers (generation, inequality, political views) to get conviction.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: inflation is is really the only way out unless you're willing to accept a crisis in these environments.
claims.claim: Since 1971 the Fed is unconstrained by gold, so governments facing political pain choose nominal inflation over market crashes; a flat nominal market hides the loss.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Again, 68 to 82, market dropped at its peak over after a 14-year window and in real terms, um, you know, 60% 55, 60%.
claims.claim: From 1968-82 the equity market fell about 55-60% in real terms yet was flat nominally.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup Larsen
claims.quote: a collection of exposures that achieve target return through a wide range of future scenarios.
claims.claim: Future Fund defines portfolio resilience as exposures achieving target return across many scenarios, with diversification, shock absorption, predictability, and protection against severe losses.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: 60 of those 82 years in decades in in consecutive decades made no money in 60/40 in real terms.
claims.claim: 60/40 delivered zero real return over 1900-1920, 1929-1949 and 1963-1982 (60 of 82 years), so it only worked after rates peaked in 1982.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: 1982 is the peak of interest rates and it went in a diagonal line for 40 years to zero, which created over 400% multiple expansion in equities alone.
claims.claim: 60/40 success since 1982 is an artifact of falling rates that created 400%+ equity multiple expansion.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we've gone from record low profit margins in 1982 to record high profit margins.
claims.claim: Profit margins are highly correlated with rates and moved from record lows in 1982 to record highs, adding to returns.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The correlation of stocks and bonds over the long run is more positively correlated than negative.
claims.claim: Over 125 years there was zero diversification benefit between stocks and bonds, and stock-bond correlation is mostly positive.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: And the 80 years that I talked about, those numbers are 0.27 and 0.26. You actually lose your sharp ratio.
claims.claim: Sharpe is ~0.35 for stocks vs 0.37 for 60/40 over 125 years, and 0.27 vs 0.26 over 1900-82, so 60/40 adds nothing.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: And because the sharp ratio for the last 40 years for S&P is 0.52 and 60/40's 0.62, you have gotten some diversification benefit, but that's simply a function of interest rates going down and being used as a tool.
claims.claim: The 60/40 diversification benefit of the last 40 years (Sharpe 0.62 vs 0.52) comes only from falling rates.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: But if we don't know where interest rates are going, it is an incredibly poor way to invest. It's dramatically suboptimal. There is no risk management.
claims.claim: 60/40 is suboptimal without a view on rates and is dangerous if rates rise, unlevered or not.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: The 60-year average 10-year bond is 5.8%.
claims.claim: 10-year yields are still below the 60-year average of 5.8%, so a structural rise in rates is a high-probability scenario.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup Larsen
claims.quote: since the first rate cut in this cycle, long-term interest rates are actually up.
claims.claim: Long rates rose after the Fed started cutting, i.e. the curve steepened.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the steepener is the best trade you can put on
claims.claim: Steepener has been the best rates trade for years, including when the curve was inverted.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: You can achieve risk-adjusted returns, and I am not exaggerating, relatively straightforward with diversification with a little bit of long ball and an and and improving your geometric returns, some value investing like Warren Buffett.
claims.claim: Diversification, a little convexity (long ball), geometric-return focus and value investing give a robust portfolio without needing alpha.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: We're talking about four times the risk-adjusted returns over 125 years.
claims.claim: Simple risk-management concepts could raise a 0.35 Sharpe several-fold; nobody does it because people extrapolate recent history.
claims.testable: partly - claim not backed by shown test

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: people just chase whatever worked the last 5 10 years and 40 years is forever for people.
claims.claim: Investors extrapolate recent performance, so they adopt 60/40 and only change after losses.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: That pool of assets has tripled in 2 years. 2 and 1/2 years.
claims.claim: Non-correlated assets (precious metals, crypto, hedge funds, options-based ETFs/structured products) tripled from ~$5T to ~$15T in 2.5 years as investors seek non-correlation.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: if we are happening to go into a period where interest rates do trend higher and there is but worse returns for assets than we've seen in the last 40 years
claims.claim: If rates trend higher with weaker asset returns for a decade, flows into non-correlated strategies should continue, since most investors only react after losses.
claims.conditions: rates rising with weak asset returns

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: There is an interaction we talked about on here of hedge fund long short equity, which is growing dramatically because of the demand for hedge fund assets.
claims.claim: Growth of long/short hedge funds plus vol compression from structured products and ETFs reflexively changes how underlying assets move.
claims.indicator: hedge fund equity exposure; vol compression

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: There was a a massive part of the structural demand that pushed this market higher was the underweight of equities of institutions having to buy back in
claims.claim: In 2025 institutional underweights forced buying back in and stable vol compression allowed risk-taking and helped policymakers after Liberation Day.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we thought it'd be a 15-ish percent type decline and then a rally.
claims.claim: The desk called the Feb-April 2025 drop (15% expected, 25% actual), bought the dip and was aggressive on the rally.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Whereas last 40 it's average is 7.1 years. Um that is because of this populist um impulse and and the political upheaval that's coming as a result of it.
claims.claim: In populist periods presidential turnover is faster (5 presidents in 1962-82, about 4 years each vs 7.1 years average in the last 40), reflecting political upheaval.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Just wait. The pitchforks are going to be on his lawn. Give it 6 to 9 months.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: Presidential elections during that '62 to '82 period, we have five of them. All five are double-digit positive with an average return of 21 and 1/2%.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the other 15 years combined have an average uh nominal performance uh of of negative 3%.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: You know what the return is at the presidential election into 2020? Or in 2020? 18 and 1/2%.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: we didn't go mining data to find this. We had this big qualitative idea, we went looked at data, and it screams at you.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: So, if you go look at '62, '66, '70, '74. Okay. All of them um were massive down years.
claims.claim: Midterm years of the populist period (1962, 66, 70, 74) were all large down years, especially over the 15 months starting in Q3 of the year before.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: the biggest drawdown of those four is 42%.
claims.claim: Midterm drawdowns in populist periods reach as much as 42%, start earlier and get bigger over time.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: by the middle of the midterm year he was in price controls as inflation picked up.

claims.speaker: Cem Karsan
claims.quote: And those pressures are the problem ultimately for equity markets.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup Larsen
claims.quote: the rise of passive investments, um which we didn't have back then.
claims.claim: Passive investing and reflexive vol suppression, new since the 1970s, could overwhelm the structural political pressures.
